A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands 4 columns to the right of the chosen anchor, wrapping around: a brick chosen at column x lands at column (x + 4) mod 8, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting network scored 0.000 on dev with both seeds, so I can't yet tell whether the problem is learning or generalisation. Until dev success rises above 0, I'll rank candidates by training success. This round follows the suggested split: (a) recipe only, (b) architecture only, (c) both. The recipe change uses 2 PPO epochs instead of 4, which gives about 1.86 times the samples. It also raises gamma to 0.97 and gae_lambda to 0.95 so the +1 exact-build bonus reaches back across episodes of 6–33 steps. The architecture change is a 2D residual CNN with height layers as channels. Each block also adds a context vector computed from the average over all cells. Each brick type gets its own small convolution the size of its footprint, giving one score per anchor cell. By my estimate it costs about 1.5 times the starting network per sample, so it gets about two-thirds as many steps.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials, and the baseline, scored 0.000 on dev with training success of 0.000. Because training success is also 0, the problem is learning itself, not generalisation. Neither more samples (229k steps at ppo_epochs 2) nor the residual CNN with global context changed that. A likely bottleneck: an exact build needs every placement right plus a DONE at the right moment. A wide stochastic policy over 257 actions almost never completes a build, so the +1 bonus is never seen. To change this, I'm pushing samples further with ppo_epochs 1 (about 426k steps on the starting network) and lowering entropy (0.003). Fewer epochs means fewer gradient steps per sample, so I'm keeping the minibatch at 128 to hold the total number of gradient steps up. The candidates are a recipe-only change, the residual CNN with the same recipe, and a new idea: a small cell transformer with footprint-conv heads, which gives global context about layers and completion.

### Round 3
All six trials score 0 on both training and dev success. That includes three recipes (2 or 1 epochs, up to 426k steps) and three families (the starting CNN, a residual CNN and a transformer). The problem is learning, not generalisation. Every trial so far shares one assumption: per-cell, translation-equivariant placement logits that rely on the described action indexing and top-left anchor. If this world indexes actions differently (for example, transposed, a different anchor or permuted cells), a convolutional head would read features from the wrong cell. That would explain why sample count and trunk choice made no difference. This round tests that assumption with non-equivariant heads that can learn any mapping from action to cell. The trials are a CNN trunk with a flat linear policy head, the starting network with a hybrid per-cell plus flat head, and a plain MLP over the flattened observation. All use the 1-epoch recipe for many samples. If any of them trains above 0, the head is the bottleneck.

### Round 4
All nine trials score exactly 0: 0 dev success and 0 training success on both seeds. That holds for a CNN, a ResCNN, a transformer, flat and hybrid heads, and a plain MLP, with between 78k and 426k steps. Fewer epochs, lower entropy and different action heads did not help, so the bottleneck is learning itself, not generalisation or the action indexing. No trial ran long (each took under 90 s), so time is not a limit. Two things remain untested. (1) A lower learning rate: every trial used 7e-4 to 1e-3, so PPO may be collapsing early. (2) Giving the network the brick's landing-layer structure directly. A per-cell network must learn "max height under the footprint, then compare with the target at that layer" from height values. A network that runs per layer and soft-selects the landing layer makes that comparison local and shared across layers. With one round left, I pair the new architecture with two recipes, and run the lower-lr recipe on the starting network so the effects can be attributed.
